newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks expected to open lower.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks expected to open lower.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open lower after Tuesday's high-tech driven selloff, analysts said.

They said that the Dow's performance will depend to some extent on DuPont Co's third quarter net, the behavior of International Business Machines Corp shares and what effect the reported settlement of a strike with the Canadian Auto Workers Union will have on shares of General Motors Corp.
"General Motors is a Dow component and it will help the average to the extent that it moves higher on the news," said Hildergard Zagorski, analyst at Prudential Securities.

"But a lot also depends on the DuPont earnings and what IBM does after the sell-off we had in high techs yesterday. On the whole, I think this market has run out of steam and is on the defensive. Still, I wouldn't rule out some firming this afternoon after a weak opening."
"We have to keep an eye on techs and bonds," she said, adding that solid third quarter earnings by Netscape Communications Corp would help the tech sector.

"I was surprised by the extent to which the over-the- counter market suffered. The tech stocks were hit really hard and we may see further pressure on that group today," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
"I'd say we go down 15 to 20 points at the opening. The market is in a technical pullback, and I think the market will remain in a trading pattern on the downside."
In Tokyo, The Nikkei Average was down 42 points at 21,082.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was down 30 points at 4027.

Among U.S. stocks, shares in General Motors edged up 1/8 to 54-3/4 while Ford Motor Co shares were up 1/8 at 31-5/8 and Chrysler Corp was unchanged at 33-5/8. Digital Equipment Corp rose 1/4 to 29-1/4, Intel Corp fell 1/4 to 105-1/4, and Texas Instruments Inc shares were up 1/8 at 51-5/8.
The dollar was strong in Tokyo and dipped in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were thinly mixed, with the long bond down 1/32 to yield 6.86 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that nine public pension funds led by the California Public Employees' Retirement System are unveiling a study that questions the fees charged by leveraged buyout firms.

The New York Times Market Place writes about initial public offerings on the Internet. W.J. Gallagher & Co will try to act as dealer in the initial public offering for a small computer company called Javelin Systems Inc.
